content: Fructooligosaccharides (FOS), also referred to as oligofructose or oligofructan, are a type of oligosaccharide that serve as an artificial or alternative sweetener. Their use became prominent in the 1980s in response to consumer demand for healthier, calorie-reduced food options. The term oligosaccharide describes short chains of sugar molecules, and in the case of FOS, these are composed of fructose molecules. The prefix oligomeans few, and saccharide refers to sugar. Chemistry Two distinct classes of FOS mixtures are commercially produced, either through the degradation of inulin or via transfructosylation processes. FOS can be derived from inulin, a polymer of D-fructose residues linked by β(2-1) bonds with a terminal α(1-2) linked D-glucose. The degree of polymerization of inulin ranges from 10 to 60. Inulin can be enzymatically or chemically degraded into a mixture of oligosaccharides with the general structure Glu-(Fru)n (GFₙ) and Frum (Fₘ), where n and m range from 1 to 7. This degradation process also occurs naturally to some extent, and these oligosaccharides are found in various plants, particularly Jerusalem artichoke and chicory. One major producer, Tienen Belgium, markets the product as oligofructose (or Raftilose), though they also market inulin under the same name, which can be confusing. Other producers include the Dutch company Cosun, which markets the product as Frutafit or Frutalose. The primary components of this class include kestose (GF₂), nystose (GF₃), fructosylnystose (GF₄), bifurcose (GF₃), inulobiose (F₂), inulotriose (F₃), and inulotetraose (F₄). The second class of FOS is prepared through the transfructosylation action of a β-fructosidase enzyme from Aspergillus niger on sucrose. The resulting mixture has the general formula GFₙ, with n ranging from 1 to 5. Unlike inulin-derived FOS, the linkages in this class are not exclusively β(1-2); other linkages are present, though in limited numbers. This class is primarily produced in Japan by Meiji Seika Kaisha. Due to the configuration of their glycosidic bonds, FOS resist hydrolysis by salivary and intestinal digestive enzymes. Instead, they are fermented by anaerobic bacteria in the colon. This property gives FOS a lower caloric value while contributing to the dietary fiber fraction of the diet. FOS are more soluble than inulins and are often used as additives in yogurt and other dairy products. They are particularly effective when combined with high-intensity artificial sweeteners, as they improve the sweetness profile and reduce aftertaste. Food Sources FOS are naturally extracted from fruits and vegetables such as bananas, onions, chicory root, garlic, asparagus, barley, wheat, jícama, tomatoes, and leeks. Jerusalem artichoke and its relative, yacón, have the highest concentrations of FOS among cultivated plants. FOS is gaining popularity in Western cultures for its prebiotic effects, as it serves as a substrate for beneficial microflora in the large intestine, promoting overall gastrointestinal health. It has also been suggested as a supplement for preventing yeast infections. The fermentation of FOS by intestinal microflora in the lower gut results in a reduced pH, which increases calcium solubility. This allows more calcium to be absorbed from food and transported into the bloodstream. FOS can be considered a small dietary fiber with low caloric value, similar to other fibers. The fermentation process produces gases and acids, with the latter providing some energy to the body. Side Effects FOS and inulin are fermented by most bacterial species in the intestine, including Klebsiella, E. coli, and various Clostridium species, which are considered less-friendly gut bacteria. These bacteria are primarily responsible for the gas formation (hydrogen and carbon dioxide) that occurs after FOS ingestion. Most individuals can tolerate 5–10 grams of FOS without experiencing gaseous discomfort, while others may experience issues with as little as 1 gram. The estimated optimal dose for adult humans is approximately 5–10 grams per day. Regulation US FDA Regulation FOS is generally recognized as safe (GRAS) by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). NZ NZFSA Regulation The New Zealand Food Safety Authority (NZFSA) has warned parents that a major European infant formula brand made in New Zealand does not comply with local regulations because it contains FOS. Parents were urged to stop using the product. While FOS has been approved in the European Union for addition in restricted amounts to infant formula (for babies up to six months) and follow-on formula (for babies between six and 12 months), these products have been sold in the EU since 1999.
